title: MOSES MET HIS WIFE AFTER HE STOOD UP FOR WOMEN BEING DRIVEN AWAY AT A WELL
paragraphs:
MOSES MET HIS WIFE AFTER HE STOOD UP FOR WOMEN BEING DRIVEN AWAY AT A WELL
He arrived in Midian as a fugitive with a shattered past. He had no throne, no reputation, and no idea that an ordinary act of courage beside a desert well was about to become part of the story God would use to rebuild his life.
There are moments when your entire life seems to collapse so quickly that you cannot imagine God could possibly be writing anything beautiful with what remains.
Moses knew that feeling.
Before there was a burning bush…
before Pharaoh heard the words, “Let My people go”…
before the Red Sea opened…
before Sinai trembled…
before Moses became one of the most recognizable figures in Scripture…
there was a frightened man sitting alone beside a well.
And that detail matters.
Because Exodus does not introduce Moses to Zipporah while Moses is powerful.
It introduces them while Moses is displaced.
He had gone from the palace of Egypt to the wilderness of Midian.
From privilege to exile.
From being somebody in Egypt to being a stranger in somebody else’s land.
And he got there carrying a scandal.
Moses had seen an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. He looked around, killed the Egyptian, and hid the body in the sand. When Pharaoh learned what happened, he sought to kill Moses.
So Moses fled.
That is where Exodus 2 takes us.
Not to a victorious Moses.
Not yet.
To a fugitive.
“Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to slay Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and dwelt in the land of Midian: and he sat down by a well.”
Exodus 2:15.
Read those final words again.
“He sat down by a well.”
He could not have known what was coming.
Maybe you understand that kind of place.
You made decisions you wish you could reverse.
Something collapsed.
A relationship ended.
Your reputation changed.
You lost something.
You ran from something.
Maybe nobody knows the whole story except you and God.
And now you are sitting emotionally in your own Midian wondering whether the most meaningful chapters of your life are already behind you.
But Moses did not know something.
The well where he sat exhausted was not the end of his story.
God was not finished.
Then seven women approached.
Scripture says they were daughters of the priest of Midian. They came to draw water and fill the troughs for their father’s flock.
Then the shepherds arrived.
And the Hebrew text gives us a detail worth slowing down for.
Exodus 2:17 says:
וַיָּבֹאוּ הָרֹעִים וַיְגָרְשׁוּם
Vayyavo’u haro‘im vaygareshum.
In context:
“The shepherds came and drove them away.”
That word translated “drove them away” comes from the Hebrew root גָּרַשׁ — garash — carrying the sense of driving out, expelling, or forcing away.
So describing the women as being harassed at the well captures the hostile character of the scene, but the precise biblical wording is even more concrete:
The shepherds drove them away.
Imagine the frustration.
The women had done the work.
They had drawn the water.
They had filled the troughs.
Then other shepherds came and pushed them away.
We are not told every detail of the confrontation, so we should not invent what Scripture does not reveal.
But Scripture tells us enough.
They were being wrongfully driven from the water they had prepared.
And Moses saw it.
Here is what is remarkable.
Moses was already carrying his own problems.
He was homeless.
He was displaced.
Pharaoh wanted him dead.
He had no visible future.
Nobody would have blamed him for thinking:
I have enough problems of my own.
But something happened when Moses watched vulnerable people being mistreated.
He stood up.
The Hebrew continues:
וַיָּקָם מֹשֶׁה וַיּוֹשִׁעָן
Vayyaqam Moshe vayoshi‘an.
“Moses rose up and helped them…”
The verb behind “helped” is especially striking.
וַיּוֹשִׁעָן — vayoshi‘an — comes from the Hebrew root יָשַׁע (yasha‘), associated with saving, delivering, or rescuing.
Moses rose.
Moses intervened.
Moses delivered them from the situation.
And then he did something wonderfully practical.
He watered their flock.
That matters.
Biblical compassion does not merely feel sorry.
It moves.
Moses did not know these women.
They could not advance his career.
He had no career.
He was not performing for an audience.
There was no crowd applauding.
No Israelite nation knew his name as deliverer yet.
No one was recording the moment for his reputation.
A broken man simply saw people being mistreated…
and stood up.
That should confront something in us.
Character is often revealed when doing the right thing offers us absolutely nothing in return.
Would you still defend someone if nobody knew?
Would you still help someone if there were no photograph?
Would you still show kindness if there were no applause?
Would you still speak when remaining silent would be easier?
Would you still serve when nobody could repay you?
Moses could not have known that the women walking toward that well were connected to the household that would become his home.
When they returned unusually early, their father asked:
“Why is it that ye are come so soon to day?”
Their answer was simple:
“An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds, and also drew water enough for us, and watered the flock.”
They did not even know the whole story of the man who had helped them.
To them, he appeared to be an Egyptian.
They did not know about the body in the sand.
They did not know Pharaoh wanted him dead.
They did not know he was running.
They did not know that the stranger beside the well had a history complicated enough to make many people uncomfortable.
They simply knew what he had done in front of them.
He helped.
Their father responded:
“And where is he? why is it that ye have left the man? call him, that he may eat bread.”
What a sentence.
Moses had fled Egypt.
Now someone was saying:
Call him.
Bring him inside.
Feed him.
There is something profoundly human about that transition.
One moment Moses is a fugitive sitting beside a well.
Soon he is sitting at a table.
Exodus continues:
“And Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter. And she bare him a son, and he called his name Gershom: for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land.”
Exodus 2:21–22.
This is where Zipporah enters Moses’ life.
Not at Pharaoh’s palace.
Not during Moses’ years of prestige.
Not after Moses had become Israel’s great leader.
She enters his story in Midian.
In exile.
In obscurity.
After failure.
After flight.
After scandal.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to understand what that means without turning the passage into a promise Scripture never makes.
The lesson is not that if you defend somebody at a well, God owes you a spouse.
The Bible does not teach that.
The lesson is deeper.
Your worst chapter does not place you beyond the reach of God’s providence.
Moses’ sin had consequences.
His exile was real.
His loneliness was real.
God did not pretend the past had never happened.
Yet Moses’ failure was not powerful enough to prevent God from continuing His purposes.
That is where this ancient story begins reaching directly into our lives.
Some people believe their usefulness to God ended when everybody discovered what they did.
Others believe it ended when the marriage failed.
When the addiction returned.
When they lost control.
When they compromised.
When they became ashamed of themselves.
When they ran.
When their carefully constructed image collapsed.
And Christianity does not answer those realities by pretending sin does not matter.
The Gospel does something infinitely better.
It tells the truth about sin…
and then tells us about a Savior greater than our sin.
Moses can point us toward themes that ultimately become glorious in Jesus Christ, but Moses himself was not Jesus.
Moses was flawed.
Jesus was sinless.
Moses needed grace.
Jesus is the One through whom grace and truth came.
Moses delivered those women from shepherds at a well.
Jesus came to accomplish a deliverance infinitely greater.
The angel announced concerning Christ:
“Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
Matthew 1:21.
The Greek word translated “save” is σώσει — sōsei — from σώζω, sōzō: to save, rescue, deliver.
And here the Gospel stops being merely an interesting comparison.
Because your deepest problem is not simply what other people have done to you.
Nor is it merely the circumstances that have driven you into your personal wilderness.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We have sinned against a holy God.
We cannot erase our guilt by becoming more religious.
We cannot bury sin deeply enough.
Moses buried the Egyptian in sand.
Human beings have been burying things ever since.
Secret habits.
Hidden messages.
Private bitterness.
Pornography.
Pride.
Jealousy.
Dishonesty.
Unforgiveness.
Religious hypocrisy.
Things deleted from phones but not from hearts.
Things hidden from spouses.
Things hidden from pastors.
Things hidden from friends.
Things we desperately hope nobody ever uncovers.
But there is no sand deep enough to hide a human heart from God.
And strangely, terrifyingly, beautifully…
that is where grace becomes breathtaking.
Because the God who completely knows you is the God who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
Jesus did not die for the imaginary version of you that never failed.
Christ died for sinners.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
That does not make sin insignificant.
The cross proves exactly how serious sin is.
Forgiveness was not purchased cheaply.
Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not God saying your rebellion never mattered.
The Gospel is God declaring that forgiveness has been made possible through the blood of His Son.
Repentance therefore is not polishing your image.
It is turning toward God.
It is dropping the disguise.
It is admitting:
Lord, I sinned.
Lord, I cannot save myself.
Lord Jesus, have mercy on me.
And maybe that is why Moses sitting beside that well feels so familiar.
Sometimes God meets people in places they never wanted to enter.
Not because every disaster is secretly pleasant.
Not because every painful circumstance was good.
Not because consequences disappear.
But because no wilderness is beyond God's reach.
Moses thought he was a stranger.
God knew his name.
Moses thought he had escaped into obscurity.
God was still writing.
Moses saw Midian.
God saw chapters Moses had not lived yet.
There would still be sheep.
Years of silence.
A burning bush.
A confrontation with Pharaoh.
A Passover night.
A sea opening.
A nation walking toward freedom.
But Moses knew none of that while sitting beside the well.
He only had the moment in front of him.
And maybe that is where faithfulness begins for you too.
You do not need to see the next twenty years.
You need to respond faithfully to Christ today.
Maybe your next act of obedience will not look spectacular.
Apologize.
Tell the truth.
Delete what keeps pulling you into sin.
Forgive.
Ask for help.
Open the Bible again.
Pray again.
Return to church.
Serve somebody who cannot repay you.
Stand beside someone being mistreated.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Come home.
And above everything else, come to Jesus.
Because Moses can inspire us…
but Moses cannot save us.
Only Christ can.
Maybe you have been carrying a private scandal so long that you have started confusing what you did with who you must always be.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending your sin never happened.
Grace rewrites your future because Jesus Christ can forgive, redeem, restore, and transform sinners who turn to Him in faith.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not scandal to pretending.
Not scandal to self-justification.
Not scandal to religious performance.
Scandal to repentance.
Scandal to mercy.
Scandal to forgiveness.
Scandal to transformation.
Scandal to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest.
There are moments when another believer needs to know they are not the only person fighting their way through Midian.
Even send it to the skeptic or unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is merely about good people pretending they never made terrible mistakes.
You may need these words on a night when the wilderness feels longer than you expected.
Salvation cannot be purchased, and grace cannot be bought.
And there is far more than one article waiting for you.
Not because clicking “Share” makes someone more spiritual.
Because somewhere in your circle may be a Moses sitting beside a well.
Someone ashamed.
Someone running.
Someone convinced the story is over.
Someone who desperately needs to hear that Christianity does not offer them permission to hide their sin.
It offers them something infinitely better.
Jesus Christ.
A Savior.
A cross.
An empty tomb.
A call to repentance.
And grace powerful enough to begin making a sinner new.
Moses arrived at that well carrying yesterday's disaster.
He walked away from it toward a future he could not yet see.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you when this article is over:

You may be sitting beside the well staring at everything you lost, while God already sees the chapters you have not lived yet—so do not make your wilderness your identity; turn your face toward Jesus and let grace have the next word.
